Read up on the history of Lindows

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linspire

Applications (and I mean native ones) must be built for a specific target platform (the CPU almost always a required part of that platform - e.g. 64-bit Windows 10).

Libraries are also built to a target platform. Application and library target platform must match, or you need a shim in the middle.

So, for example, DirectX libraries. If they existed for Linux then Linux applications could use that library. Microsoft obviously won't go and build DirectX for Linux, or make a shim. Someone else can try to make a library that acts just like DirectX, or a shim that lets Linux talk to DirectX the way DirectX expects and vice versa.

So this is what WINE does, provide shims and replacement libraries, which must be reverse engineered from study of the original ones, and which must include all possible bugs, side effects, undocumented effects, etc. of the original to be 100% compatible.

Since Windows is always changing and since new technologies are always coming out, it's a moving target for reverse engineering efforts.

Nothing stopping anyone from making a distro that includes WINE but it's not hard to install it on any existing distro, and in the case of "shims", it's illegal to include Windows libraries without Microsoft's permission.
